title: Secatogues
summary: Secatogue is used in older sources for a south-shore Native community and place-name region east of Massapequa. Its history belongs with tidal creeks, Great South Bay travel, fishing and shellfish places, kinship, neighboring communities, regional diplomacy, and colonial land pressure.
map_geometry_source: Restored from prior WP Go Maps Secatogue Ancestral Land polygon for broad community and territory context; not a camp, village, shell-heap, burial, or private-property location.
why_this_matters: The Secatogue people historically maintained numerous thriving village sites along the tidal creeks flowing into the Great South Bay, where they actively harvested the region's rich marine resources. Recognizing their deep connection to this "dark colored land" demonstrates how early Indigenous communities built complex, sustainable economies uniquely adapted to Long Island's specific coastal ecosystems.
history_content:
Seventeenth-century records place Secatogue within a wider western Long Island political landscape. Tackapousha appears in Dutch records as an alliance figure connected with Massapequa and neighboring communities, including Secatogue, during a period of intense colonial expansion.

This history should not be reduced to land sales. It includes adaptation, negotiation, foodways, waterways, and community survival under pressure from disease, warfare, deeds, and colonial courts.
translation_content: Secatogue translates to “the black or dark colored land.”
preservation_content: Camp, village, shell-heap, burial, and private-property locations are described broadly to keep attention on Secatogue history, waterways, and community landscapes.
